source.title: MSE loss does not generate superposition

record.file_problem: The post's prose is substantially present, but many equations and mathematical symbols are missing from the extracted text, and the referenced embedding plots are not included. The text is not cut off and is the correct document.
record.tranche_reason: The authors report toy autoencoder experiments and mathematical comparisons that qualify the claim: under their MSE setup, superposition is not consistently favored and can have the same minimum loss as orthogonal encodings. Results also differ across loss functions and settings.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the authors' autoencoder experiments, their stated exact mathematical comparisons, and their own initial observation about input noise. The post's opening references to results from other work are cited findings, so they are not rows. The embedding plots and many equations are missing from the supplied text; outcomes are recorded only where the prose states them. A commenter reports a separate experiment, which is not attributed to the post's authors and is not included as a study result.
record.test_reason: The authors' own toy autoencoder experiments and exact loss calculations show whether superposition emerges depending on the loss function. This qualifies V1: superposition in small networks depends on the training objective. The setup differs from the original, which used linear encoding with ReLU output and importance-weighted loss.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors argue that plain MSE gives no incentive for superposition, so outcomes depend on initialization and other pressures, and they recommend CE, or L4 where CE does not apply. They acknowledge that the math is incomplete, and the equal-loss result is shown only for small cases.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains linear autoencoders to reconstruct z-hot inputs and compares MSE, BCE, L4, and CE. It does not reproduce the original method; the authors also discuss the original work's use of a modified effective loss rather than plain MSE.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported geometry varies with loss function and with the tested T, D, and z settings; BCE is described as changing from successful superposition at T=3 to giving up at larger T.

fits_no_version.finding: In the author's computation-in-superposition experiments, input noise made each circuit use as few neurons as possible. The expected trade-off that would preserve superposition did not appear.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under MSE training, input noise drives circuits onto minimal neuron sets rather than toward superposed allocations.

record.problems: The embedding outcomes are described qualitatively and the referenced plots are missing from the supplied text; the experiment reports five runs per configuration but no uncertainty estimates or numerical geometry measures. Many mathematical expressions are missing from the extraction. The authors themselves describe the mathematical argument as incomplete and note assumptions and cases they did not investigate.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Cited findings from earlier work and a separate experiment reported in a comment were not treated as results of this post's authors.

untested.parts: The sparsity-dependent phase transition (only z=1 and z=2 with uniform frequencies), the role of feature importance, ReLU-output models as in the original, and regular geometry beyond small symmetric cases.

missing.what: An analytic result that random-vector superposition gives higher MSE than the orthogonal encodings (L_sup > L_orth) at general T, D and z. This is a further case of no MSE advantage for superposition.
A cross-loss statement that, at z=1, MSE is the only loss without a clear embedding pattern.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label for MSE is downgraded to limits_scope. The original Toy Models used importance-weighted MSE with a ReLU output, and itself found that purely linear models do not superpose. The post notes that the original modified the loss. A linear model trained with MSE therefore qualifies when superposition emerges rather than showing it absent where V1 predicts it. The plots and equations are missing from the supplied text, so all experimental states are qualitative. A commenter's P-exponent experiment is not the authors' work and is excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not establish a general sparsity-dependent transition or show that feature importance determines the geometry. Its experiments use the stated T, D and z settings and compare loss functions.
The post does not test whether neuron polysemanticity arises from capacity competition or whether more important features get dedicated dimensions.
The post does not investigate other causes of polysemantic neurons.
The post does not test feature representations in LLMs or use dictionary learning or SAEs.
The post does not test whether dictionary features are complete, stable, or canonical.
The post uses and discusses individual feature embedding vectors but does not compare one-dimensional features against multi-dimensional features.

rows.subject: linear autoencoder (T=3, 4, or 5; D=2)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on all possible z-hot feature vectors with MSE loss; five runs per configuration.
rows.measure: Visual geometry of the learned embedding vectors and apparent superposition
rows.value: MSE embeddings were very varied; vectors were commonly nearly on top of each other, and MSE did not consistently produce superposition.
rows.note: The post reports the z=1 configurations together, not separate outcomes for each configuration. It describes the plots in prose, but the plots themselves are absent.
rows.check: MSE embeddings varied across seeds: superposition was sometimes present by chance from initialization, not consistently. This is acceptable as partial, but note there is no nonlinearity at the output, unlike the original.

rows.subject: linear autoencoder (T=4 or 5, D=2)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on all possible z-hot feature vectors with BCE loss; five runs per configuration.
rows.measure: Visual geometry and which features were represented
rows.value: For larger T, networks gave up on superposition, represented two features approximately orthogonally, and did not represent the others.
rows.note: The post groups the larger-T configurations together and does not give separate outcomes.
rows.check: At T=4 and T=5, BCE represented two features orthogonally and dropped the rest. That is no superposition, not a partial version of it.

rows.subject: linear autoencoder (T=3, 4, or 5; D=2)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on all possible z-hot feature vectors with L4 loss; five runs per configuration.
rows.value: L4 networks avoid negative correlations as much as positive correlations.
rows.note: The post says this behavior is expected because L4 penalizes positive and negative interference equally. It does not separately describe each z=1 configuration.
rows.check: Avoiding positive and negative correlations equally describes interference symmetry. It does not report whether superposition was present; the post only implies L4 gives a 'clear pattern' at z=1.

rows.operation_detail: Introduced noise in the input during experiments representing tiny circuits.

conditions.value: introduced; comparison setting without noise is implied but not specified
represent more tiny circuits than hidden-layer neurons; only one or a few circuits computed per forward pass

rows.measure: Number of neurons used per circuit
rows.value: Input noise caused each circuit to be distributed over a much smaller number of neurons; the network did not seem to preserve superposition as the author expected.

relationships.condition: Plain MSE with a linear readout, linear autoencoder, z=1 (experiments and exact calculations for T=3/D=2 and T=4/D=3)
relationships.reason: MSE embeddings were varied with no consistent superposition (R1), and the best superposition loss exactly equals the orthogonal loss (R8, R9). Emergence therefore depends on the loss function; this does not contradict the original, which used a different loss and a ReLU output.
relationships.display_finding: MSE embeddings varied without consistent superposition, and the best superposition loss exactly equalled the orthogonal loss, so emergence depended on the loss. This does not contradict the original, which used a different loss and a ReLU output.
